""**The Weight of the Cage**

The night air in Darwin was thick with the scent of salt and diesel, the kind of humidity that clung to skin like a second layer. Dale Scott Walkinshaw had always hated that feeling—the way the heat made his thoughts sluggish, his movements slow, as if the world itself were pressing down on him. But tonight, the weight was different. It was the girl in his arms, her breath shallow, her body trembling against the wreckage of the Hilux. The palm tree had split the bonnet like an axe through kindling, and the only sound now was the distant wail of sirens, growing louder.

Dale didn’t remember much about the crash. He remembered the bar—the neon glow of the beer signs, the way the woman had laughed when he’d stumbled over his words. He remembered the taste of rum, the burn of it, the way it had dulled the edges of the voices in his head. The ones that told him he was worthless. The ones that had been there since he was a kid, since the foster homes, since the first time a cop had looked at him like he was already guilty of something.

The sirens stopped. Boots crunched on gravel. Flashlights cut through the dark, painting the scene in harsh white strokes.

‘Step away from her, mate,’ a voice said. Not unkind, but firm. Dale looked up. Two officers—one tall, broad-shouldered, the other younger, his face tight with the kind of wariness Dale knew well. He’d seen it before. In the eyes of social workers. In the mirrors of police stations.

‘She’s hurt,’ Dale said, his voice rough. ‘I didn’t mean—’

‘Hands where we can see ’em.’

The next part was a blur. The girl was taken away in an ambulance, her name still unknown to him. Dale was patted down, cuffed, guided toward the back of a caged police van. The metal smelled of sweat and disinfectant. The door clanged shut behind him, the sound echoing in his skull.

He wasn’t afraid of the cage. He’d been in worse. But the voices were louder now, sharper. *You messed up. Again. You always do.*

Dale pressed his forehead against the cold bars, trying to breathe. The van started moving, the motion making his stomach lurch. He closed his eyes, but all he saw was the girl’s face, the way her lips had turned blue in the glow of the flashlights.

Then the thoughts came, the ones that had been gnawing at him for years. *What’s the point?*

He’d tried before. In the lockup in Katherine, after they’d held him for stealing a six-pack. In the back of another van, two years ago, when the cops had picked him up for sleeping on a park bench. He’d banged his head against the bars until the world went black, waking up to a paramedic slapping his cheeks. They’d laughed at him then. Called him a drama queen.

But tonight, the urge was different. Quieter. More certain.

Dale slipped off his belt. The leather was worn, the buckle loose. He looped it through the bars, testing the give. The van hit a pothole, and he nearly lost his balance. His fingers fumbled, slick with sweat.

No one was watching. There were no cameras. There never were.

He thought of the report, gathering dust in some office—*16 attempts*. Six of them almost successful. Six people who had been left to choke, to bleed, to slip away in the dark. And now him.

The belt tightened around his neck. His vision spotted. For a moment, he thought he heard his mother’s voice—the real one, not the one in his head. The one from the few memories he had of her, before the system swallowed him whole. *You’re better than this,* she’d said once, her hand warm on his shoulder.

But the voices were louder.

The van turned a corner. The belt dug in.

And then—nothing.

---

When the officers opened the back door twenty minutes later, they found him slumped against the bars, his face pale, his lips parted as if he’d been about to speak. The younger cop vomited into the gutter. The older one radioed it in, his voice steady, practiced.

‘Another one,’ he said.

At the station, the sergeant sighed and filled out the paperwork. Another death in custody. Another file to be buried under bureaucracy. Another name added to a list no one wanted to read.

In the coroner’s office, Greg Cavanagh would later write that it wasn’t a matter of *if*, but *when*. But in the quiet of that Darwin night, as the van was hosed out and the belt was tossed into an evidence bag, no one said a word about the boy who had just wanted the voices to stop.

No one mentioned the girl in the hospital, waking up to the news that the man who had held her as she bled would never hold anyone again.

And no one asked why, in a system that knew this would happen, the cages had no eyes."""
